record.paper_title: Open problems in Euclidean Ramsey Theory
record.original_question: For every integer n, must every set of 2^(n-2)+1 points in the plane in general position, meaning no three points are collinear, contain n points that are the vertices of a convex n-gon?

evidence.quote: Any set of 2^{n-2} + 1 points in the plane in general position
must contain the vertices of a convex n-gon

artifact.self_contained_problem:
A finite set of points in the Euclidean plane is said to be in general position if no three of its points are collinear. A set of n points is said to form a convex n-gon if the points are the vertices of a convex polygon (equivalently, none of the points lies in the convex hull of the others).

Prove or disprove the following: for every integer n ≥ 3, every set of 2^(n−2) + 1 points in the plane in general position contains n points that are the vertices of a convex n-gon.
artifact.status_search_result: The Erdős–Szekeres conjecture ES(n) = 2^(n−2)+1 is verified for n ≤ 6 (the case n = 6 by Szekeres and Peters, 2006) and remains open for n ≥ 7. Suk (2016) proved the upper bound ES(n) ≤ 2^{n+o(n)}, later refined to 2^n + O(√n log n) by Holmsen–Mojarrad–Pach–Tardos. The exact conjectured value is still unproven in general.

status_evidence.title: Happy ending problem - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: Conjecture verified for n ≤ 6; open for larger n.
status_evidence.claim: The exact conjecture is verified up to n=6 and open in general.

status_evidence.title: On the Erdős–Szekeres convex polygon problem (Suk, 2016)
status_evidence.snippet: Suk proved ES(n) ≤ 2^{n+o(n)}, close to the conjectured bound but not matching it.
status_evidence.claim: Best known upper bound is near-optimal but does not prove the conjecture.

status_evidence.title: The Erdős–Szekeres Conjecture Revisited
status_evidence.snippet: Recent work (2025) revisits the conjecture, indicating it remains open.
status_evidence.claim: The conjecture is still an active open problem as of 2025.
